title: 2026-27 Budget Passed: $359.2M Balanced
summary: Nauru's Parliament passed the 2026-27 Appropriation Bill on 20 July 2026 — a balanced budget projecting $359.2 million in revenue against $359.0 million in managed expenditure.
author: Republic of Nauru Editorial Team

body.heading: Budget at a Glance
body.content:
The Government of Nauru has delivered a balanced budget for the 2026-27 fiscal year, themed "Capitalising on the Current High Revenue Environment: Investing in the People and a Productive Future."

The official figures published by the Department of Finance project total revenue of $359.2 million against managed expenditure of $359.0 million — a small surplus. The budget prioritises long-term national development rather than short-term consumption.

A Supply Budget was in place from 1 July to 20 July 2026 to allow the Government time to finalise key negotiations for the main appropriation. The main appropriation was officially passed on 20 July 2026 and became effective from 21 July 2026. Expenditures authorised during the supply period are formally charged against the full-year Appropriation Act.

body.heading: What Is New in This Year's Budget Papers
body.content:
The 2026-27 budget papers introduce several structural changes aimed at greater transparency and strategic foresight:

1. A brief review of fiscal performance for FY 2025-26
2. The introduction of a Medium-Term Debt Strategy covering 2026-2030 — a new requirement under Nauru's new Government Debt Act
3. A dedicated section in Budget Paper 1 outlining Central Treasury (overall) fiscal risks
4. A detailed analysis of fiscal risks pertaining to Public Enterprises, covered under Budget Paper 2 Part III (PEMU and Public Enterprises)

These additions reflect a shift toward longer-horizon fiscal planning, which matters for a small island economy where revenue sources can shift quickly.

body.heading: Why the Revenue Environment Matters
body.content:
The budget theme explicitly references a "high revenue environment." For Nauru, that environment is shaped by a small number of concentrated revenue streams — principally fishing licence fees under the Parties to the Nauru Agreement, residual phosphate earnings, development partner support, and taxation.

Because the revenue base is narrow, the introduction of a formal Medium-Term Debt Strategy is significant: it gives the Government a published framework for managing borrowing across multiple years rather than on an annual basis. The budget papers are published in full by the Department of Finance, including the Appropriation Bill, Budget Papers 1 and 2, and Development Fund Projections.

body.heading: What This Means for Visitors
body.content:
For travellers, national budgets translate into practical conditions on the ground — road maintenance, water supply, electricity reliability, and public services.

A balanced budget with a formal multi-year debt strategy suggests continuity rather than abrupt cuts to public spending. Visitors should still expect the practical realities of a small island state: infrastructure works can cause localised disruption, and service availability can vary by district.

If you are planning a trip, the most useful takeaway is that official budget documentation is publicly available. If a specific project affects your plans — a road upgrade, a water facility, an airport-adjacent development — you can check the published budget papers directly rather than relying on secondary summaries.

body.heading: Where to Verify This Information
body.content:
All figures in this article come from the Nauru Department of Finance's official 2026-27 budget page, which publishes the Budget Speech, Budget Papers 1 and 2, the Appropriation Bill, and Development Fund Projections as downloadable documents.

Budget figures are frequently misreported in secondary sources — including, previously, on this site. We have corrected our coverage and now cite the Department of Finance directly. If you need the authoritative numbers, always consult the primary documents.

title: Nauru Sets Out Climate Adaptation Priorities to 2035
summary: Nauru's updated Nationally Determined Contribution outlines coastal resilience priorities through 2035, alongside the GEF-backed CARE4N coastal protection project.
author: Republic of Nauru Editorial Team

body.heading: The Scale of the Problem
body.content:
Climate change is not a distant threat for Nauru — it is an immediate and accelerating reality. The island's maximum elevation is just 65 metres, and the majority of the population and critical infrastructure sits along a narrow coastal belt.

Rising sea levels, intensified storm surges, and coastal erosion threaten roads, homes, the airport, and government infrastructure that sits within metres of the shoreline. For a nation of roughly 21 square kilometres, there is very little inland space to retreat to.

body.heading: The CARE4N Coastal Resilience Project
body.content:
Nauru's most concrete coastal protection effort is the Coastal Area Resilience Enhancement for Nauru project — CARE4N — supported through the Global Environment Facility (GEF) with the Asian Development Bank as implementing agency.

The project's objective is that Nauru's coastal assets and ecosystems enjoy improved protection in an integrated, affordable, sustainable, adaptive, equitable, and replicable manner. Funding comprises a GEF allocation of USD 2,660,600 together with USD 1,000,000 in co-financing.

Importantly, Nauru's own climate documentation acknowledges that CARE4N will not cover the full cost of implementing all recommended hard and nature-based solutions — meaning the project is a starting point rather than a complete coastal defence programme.

body.heading: Updated Nationally Determined Contribution (2025-2035)
body.content:
Nauru has submitted an updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) covering 2025 to 2035 under the Paris Agreement. The document sets out the country's adaptation and mitigation priorities for the coming decade and is published in full on the UNFCCC website.

The NDC is the authoritative statement of what Nauru itself commits to and requests. It is a more reliable basis for understanding national climate policy than secondary reporting, because it is the document Nauru formally submits to the international process.

body.heading: Adaptation Approaches Under Discussion
body.content:
Alongside engineered coastal protection, Nauru's adaptation planning has included discussion of managed relocation of people and assets toward the island's higher interior (the Topside phosphate plateau) — an approach that reflects the reality that in some locations, defending the coastline may not be feasible indefinitely.

Other measures under consideration across Pacific island states include natural coastal buffers such as native vegetation and coral rubble berms, and early-warning systems for storm surges and king tides. Nauru's specific mix of measures is set out in its NDC and project documentation.

body.heading: What This Means for Visitors
body.content:
For visitors, climate adaptation work has practical implications:

- Coastal construction and protection works can cause localised access restrictions and minor traffic disruption — ask at your accommodation about current conditions
- Some beach access points may be affected by works; conditions change, so check locally rather than relying on older guides
- The Topside plateau offers the island's most dramatic landscapes and is worth visiting for its own sake

Nauru remains a destination where conditions are best confirmed locally on arrival. Treat any travel guide — including this one — as a starting point, not a substitute for current local information.

body.heading: Where to Verify This Information
body.content:
The primary sources for this article are the Global Environment Facility's project page for CARE4N (project ID 11705) and Nauru's Updated Nationally Determined Contribution 2025-2035, published on the UNFCCC website.

Earlier versions of this article cited a "$500 million Pacific Island Forum Climate Adaptation Fund" with an "$18 million allocation to Nauru." We could not verify those figures against any official source, and they have been removed.

title: Nauru Visitor Numbers Up 94% Year-on-Year
summary: Nauru recorded a 94% increase in tourist numbers in 2024 compared with 2023 — a significant shift for one of the world's least-visited countries.
author: Republic of Nauru Editorial Team

body.heading: A Significant Shift for a Rarely-Visited Destination
body.content:
Nauru has long held the distinction of being among the least-visited countries on Earth, with visitor numbers historically measured in the low hundreds per year. That picture has been changing.

In 2024, Nauru recorded an approximately 94% increase in tourist numbers compared with 2023, according to statements from the Nauru Tourism Corporation reported by international travel media. The corporation noted that traveller curiosity about the country had never been higher.

The increase is measured from a very small base — which means percentage growth figures can look dramatic while absolute visitor numbers remain modest. That context matters when interpreting the numbers.

body.heading: Why Interest Is Growing
body.content:
Several factors appear to be driving interest in Nauru as a destination:

- Curiosity about the world's smallest republic and one of its least-visited nations
- Its unusual history — phosphate mining, wartime occupation, and a distinctive modern political story
- Diving and snorkelling on coral reefs that see very little recreational pressure
- The dramatic Topside phosphate plateau, which has no real equivalent elsewhere
- Improved awareness through travel media coverage of the country's rising visitor numbers

Nauru is not a conventional resort destination. There is one main hotel, limited public transport, and few organised tours. Visitors who come tend to be independent travellers seeking somewhere genuinely unusual.

body.heading: Practical Realities for Visitors
body.content:
Growth in visitor numbers does not change the island's fundamentals, and travellers should plan accordingly:

- Accommodation is limited — book before you book flights, not after
- Flights are infrequent and route through Brisbane or Nadi
- Public transport is minimal; most visitors use taxis or arrange transport through their accommodation
- Cash in Australian dollars is essential — card acceptance is limited and ATMs are unreliable
- Services and opening hours can vary; confirm locally on arrival

Nauru rewards preparation. The practical constraints are real, but they are also part of why the island remains genuinely off the beaten track.

body.heading: Where to Verify This Information
body.content:
The 94% growth figure originates from statements by the Nauru Tourism Corporation, reported by eGlobal Travel Media in August 2024. The figure refers to 2024 performance against 2023.

Earlier versions of this article described a "Nauru Eco-Tourism Initiative" with a "$3.2 million AUD SPTO grant" and specific programme targets. We were unable to verify those details against any official source, and they have been removed. If you need current tourism statistics, contact the Nauru Tourism Corporation directly.
